Lecture 43

Green kernels for diffusion and distributed sources

We derive the free diffusion kernel and prove its point initial trace. We combine initial data with a distributed source, prove uniqueness in a bounded class, and choose a kernel that satisfies the spatial boundary conditions.

By the end of this lecture you will be able to:

  • Derive the free kernel with the unitary Fourier convention and verify its initial trace.
  • Prove uniqueness for classical solutions bounded on each finite closed time strip.
  • Distinguish initial propagation from causal forcing and solve a switched-source problem.
  • Construct the absorbing half-line kernel and compare free and interval boundaries.

A release at one point spreads under diffusion. A source that stays on adds new releases at every later time. Part IV begins by constructing the kernels that describe both effects. The stages are free diffusion and its initial trace (Section 43.1), bounded uniqueness and causal sources (Sections 43.2–43.4), and images and interval kernels (Sections 43.5–43.6). The last stage connects the whole line to Lecture 37’s finite rod.

43.2 Initial data and bounded uniqueness

A continuous initial field differs from a point release. Bounded uniformly continuous data need not have a finite integral on the line. Write ∥u0∥∞=sup⁡x∈R∣u0(x)∣\norm{u_0}_\infty=\sup_{x\in\R}\abs{u_0(x)}∥u0​∥∞​=supx∈R​∣u0​(x)∣.

43.3 A causal source kernel

A distributed source creates material at a range of positions and times. For heat, the equation in normalized form is ut−Duxx=f,f=gρcp,D=κρcp,u_t-Du_{xx}=f,\qquad f=\frac{g}{\rho c_{\mathrm p}}, \qquad D=\frac\kappa{\rho c_{\mathrm p}},ut​−Duxx​=f,f=ρcp​g​,D=ρcp​κ​,(43.13) where ggg (not the profile gDg_DgD​), ρ\rhoρ, cpc_{\mathrm p}cp​ and κ\kappaκ are Lecture 37’s heat production, material density, specific heat and conductivity. For a concentration, fff is directly the amount created per unit length and unit time.

Definition 43.6 (Causal source kernel). The causal source kernel on the line is Gfree(x,t;ξ,τ)={0,t<τ,Kfree(x,t;ξ,τ),t>τ.G_{\mathrm{free}}(x,t;\xi,\tau)= \begin{cases} 0,&t<\tau,\\ K_{\mathrm{free}}(x,t;\xi,\tau),&t>\tau. \end{cases}Gfree​(x,t;ξ,τ)={0,Kfree​(x,t;ξ,τ),​t<τ,t>τ.​(43.14) Its value at t=τt=\taut=τ is immaterial. The notation Gfree=Θ(t−τ)KfreeG_{\mathrm{free}}=\Heaviside(t-\tau)K_{\mathrm{free}}Gfree​=Θ(t−τ)Kfree​ means this causal extension, not a prescribed function value for KfreeK_{\mathrm{free}}Kfree​ at t=τt=\taut=τ.

The kernel is locally integrable in space-time. Indeed, its absolute integral over a compact rectangle is bounded by the length of that rectangle’s time interval, because its spatial integral at each t>τt>\taut>τ is 111. 43.5 Images on a half-line

An absorbing end removes material that reaches it. Its concentration condition is the zero Dirichlet value u(0,t)=0u(0,t)=0u(0,t)=0. For x≥0x\ge0x≥0 and ξ>0\xi>0ξ>0 the method of images defines the image kernel by K+(x,t;ξ,τ)=gD(x−ξ,t−τ)−gD(x+ξ,t−τ),t>τ.K_+(x,t;\xi,\tau)=g_D(x-\xi,t-\tau)-g_D(x+\xi,t-\tau),\qquad t>\tau.K+​(x,t;ξ,τ)=gD​(x−ξ,t−τ)−gD​(x+ξ,t−τ),t>τ.(43.28) The negative image at −ξ-\xi−ξ enforces the zero boundary. Figure 43.1 shows that cancellation and the remaining field on x≥0x\ge0x≥0.

K+(x,t;ξ,τ)=gD(x−ξ,t−τ)−gD(x+ξ,t−τ),t>τ.K_+(x,t;\xi,\tau)=g_D(x-\xi,t-\tau)-g_D(x+\xi,t-\tau),\qquad t>\tau.K+​(x,t;ξ,τ)=gD​(x−ξ,t−τ)−gD​(x+ξ,t−τ),t>τ.(43.28)

Proposition 43.9 (The half-line kernel). Extend u0u_0u0​ oddly to the line, with value zero at the origin. This extension is bounded and uniformly continuous. Across the origin, bound the difference by ∣u0(x)−u0(0)∣+∣u0(−y)−u0(0)∣\abs{u_0(x)-u_0(0)}+\abs{u_0(-y)-u_0(0)}∣u0​(x)−u0​(0)∣+∣u0​(−y)−u0​(0)∣ for x≥0≥yx\ge0\ge yx≥0≥y. Theorem 43.5 gives the free evolution of this extension. Splitting its integral at ξ=0\xi=0ξ=0 gives (43.29). The resulting field is odd, so it vanishes at 000. The same comparison proof on [0,R][0,R][0,R], with zero data at 000, gives uniqueness in the stated bounded class. ■

43.6 The interval kernel and images

A finite rod with both ends held at zero needs a kernel that vanishes at both ends. For L>0L>0L>0, 0≤x,ξ≤L0\le x,\xi\le L0≤x,ξ≤L and t>τt>\taut>τ, Lecture 37’s kernel is Kint(x,t;ξ,τ)=2L∑n=1∞e−D(nπ/L)2(t−τ)sin⁡nπxLsin⁡nπξL.K_{\mathrm{int}}(x,t;\xi,\tau)=\frac2L\sum_{n=1}^\infty \ee^{-D(n\pi/L)^2(t-\tau)}\sin\frac{n\pi x}L\sin\frac{n\pi\xi}L.Kint​(x,t;ξ,τ)=L2​n=1∑∞​e−D(nπ/L)2(t−τ)sinLnπx​sinLnπξ​.(43.32) Each sine mode solves the heat equation and vanishes at both ends. The Gaussian restricted to (0,L)(0,L)(0,L) does not have these boundary values. For an interior smooth compact test, Lecture 32 gives absolutely summable sine coefficients. Pairing (43.32) with the test multiplies those coefficients by e−D(nπ/L)2h\ee^{-D(n\pi/L)^2h}e−D(nπ/L)2h, with h=t−τ>0h=t-\tau>0h=t−τ>0. The absolute coefficient sum controls the tail uniformly in hhh. Letting h↓0h\downarrow0h↓0 therefore recovers the test’s sine series at ξ\xiξ, proving the interior point trace.

Kint(x,t;ξ,τ)=2L∑n=1∞e−D(nπ/L)2(t−τ)sin⁡nπxLsin⁡nπξL.K_{\mathrm{int}}(x,t;\xi,\tau)=\frac2L\sum_{n=1}^\infty \ee^{-D(n\pi/L)^2(t-\tau)}\sin\frac{n\pi x}L\sin\frac{n\pi\xi}L.Kint​(x,t;ξ,τ)=L2​n=1∑∞​e−D(nπ/L)2(t−τ)sinLnπx​sinLnπξ​.(43.32)

Lecture 37 proves that, for piecewise continuous initial data and continuous bounded normalized source f=g/(ρcp)f=g/(\rho c_{\mathrm p})f=g/(ρcp​), the two-term formula (43.17), with KintK_{\mathrm{int}}Kint​ and spatial integrals over (0,L)(0,L)(0,L), equals the modal series. Without a source it gives the unique solution with mean-square initial values. Continuous piecewise C1C^1C1 data vanishing at the ends give the unique classical solution. With a source, classical regularity still needs the data checks described there. Kernels with zero end values need not preserve total amount.

Pair a point release at ξ\xiξ with its negative image at −ξ-\xi−ξ, then repeat the pair with spatial period 2L2L2L. The resulting image series is Kimg(x,t;ξ,τ)=∑n∈Z[gD(x−ξ+2nL,t−τ)−gD(x+ξ+2nL,t−τ)].K_{\mathrm{img}}(x,t;\xi,\tau)=\sum_{n\in\Z} \bigl[g_D(x-\xi+2nL,t-\tau)-g_D(x+\xi+2nL,t-\tau)\bigr].Kimg​(x,t;ξ,τ)=n∈Z∑​[gD​(x−ξ+2nL,t−τ)−gD​(x+ξ+2nL,t−τ)].(43.33) For fixed 0<δ<H<∞0<\delta<H<\infty0<δ<H<∞, the series and its fixed-order derivatives in xxx and ttt converge uniformly on [0,L]2×{δ≤t−τ≤H}[0,L]^2\times\{\delta\le t-\tau\le H\}[0,L]2×{δ≤t−τ≤H}. Indeed, Gaussian differentiation gives, for fixed nonnegative integers jjj and mmm, constants C,c>0C,c>0C,c>0 such that, for ∣n∣≥2\abs n\ge2∣n∣≥2 on this set, ∣∂xj∂hmgD(x±ξ+2nL,h)∣≤C(1+∣n∣)j+2me−cn2,h=t−τ.\abs{\partial_x^j\partial_h^m g_D(x\mathbin{\pm}\xi+2nL,h)} \le C(1+\abs n)^{j+2m}\ee^{-cn^2},\qquad h=t-\tau.​∂xj​∂hm​gD​(x±ξ+2nL,h)​≤C(1+∣n∣)j+2me−cn2,h=t−τ.(43.34) Here ∣x±ξ+2nL∣≥2L(∣n∣−1)\abs{x\mathbin{\pm}\xi+2nL}\ge2L(\abs n-1)∣x±ξ+2nL∣≥2L(∣n∣−1) and the powers of h−1h^{-1}h−1 are bounded by the lower elapsed-time cutoff. The majorant is summable. Lecture 32’s termwise differentiation lemma therefore makes the sum a smooth heat solution for positive elapsed time.

Kimg(x,t;ξ,τ)=∑n∈Z[gD(x−ξ+2nL,t−τ)−gD(x+ξ+2nL,t−τ)].K_{\mathrm{img}}(x,t;\xi,\tau)=\sum_{n\in\Z} \bigl[g_D(x-\xi+2nL,t-\tau)-g_D(x+\xi+2nL,t-\tau)\bigr].Kimg​(x,t;ξ,τ)=n∈Z∑​[gD​(x−ξ+2nL,t−τ)−gD​(x+ξ+2nL,t−τ)].(43.33)

Absolute convergence permits reindexing. At x=0x=0x=0 the direct term with index nnn equals the image term with index −n-n−n, because gDg_DgD​ is even. At x=Lx=Lx=L it equals the image term with index −n−1-n-1−n−1. Both boundary values are zero. For a fixed interior ξ\xiξ and a compactly supported interior test, the term gD(x−ξ,h)g_D(x-\xi,h)gD​(x−ξ,h) has the required delta trace. Every other image center has a positive separation from the test support. For large ∣n∣\abs n∣n∣ this separation grows at least linearly in ∣n∣\abs n∣n∣. Their pairings are therefore bounded by sums of Ch−1/2e−c(1+n2)/hC h^{-1/2}\ee^{-c(1+n^2)/h}Ch−1/2e−c(1+n2)/h, which tend to zero as h↓0h\downarrow0h↓0. Indeed, splitting each exponential into equal factors bounds one with h≤Hh\le Hh≤H by a summable Gaussian in nnn, while h−1/2e−c/(2h)→0h^{-1/2}\ee^{-c/(2h)}\to0h−1/2e−c/(2h)→0 controls the other. This proves the interior point trace of the image series.

The image construction and the sine series meet the same boundary and initial requirements. Lecture 56 will prove their equality by applying them to common continuous compatible initial data and using uniqueness. The present comparison identifies which boundary problem each kernel serves without assuming that equality.

Summary

A diffusion propagator carries initial data forward from one time. Its causal extension supplies the response to a source at each space-time point. The free Gaussian, the absorbing half-line kernel and the interval kernel serve different spatial boundary conditions.

  • Free propagation: gD(z,h)=η2Dh(z)g_D(z,h)=\eta_{\sqrt{2Dh}}(z)gD​(z,h)=η2Dh​​(z) has unit mass, centered second moment 2Dh2Dh2Dh and a point distributional trace.

  • Uniqueness: comparison proves uniqueness for classical solutions bounded on each finite closed time strip. Point releases lie outside that class at their initial time.

  • Forcing: bounded uniformly continuous u0u_0u0​ and bounded fff with a continuous extension from each open slab to its closure give the weak identity. Jointly continuous, bounded fff, fxf_xfx​ and fxxf_{xx}fxx​ on each open slab, with bounds up to its ends, give the classical PDE there.

  • Boundaries: a negative image enforces a zero end value and permits loss of amount. Two zero ends require the interval kernel or its image construction.

Lecture 44 interprets diffusion kernels through probability and relates boundary loss to a probability current.

Cited proofs: L. C. Evans, Partial Differential Equations, 2nd ed., §2.3.3(a), p. 57, citing F. John, Partial Differential Equations, 4th ed., Ch. 7, for nonuniqueness without a growth restriction.

Reading: T. Myint-U and L. Debnath, Linear Partial Differential Equations for Scientists and Engineers, 4th ed., §12.4, Example 12.4.3, and §§12.6, 12.15 (half-line and finite transforms); R. S. Strichartz, A Guide to Distribution Theory and Fourier Transforms, §5.2 and the Dirichlet image and source problems in §5.5; Evans, §2.3.1 and §4.3.1, Example 2 (heat kernel, data, forcing and Fourier construction).
